title: Fortified Wine from Port to Pineau
summary: Makers add strong grape spirit to keep these wines safe and shape their taste, and British sea trade made port, sherry and Madeira famous, while Pineau des Charentes grew up on farms in the west of France.

blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Today we learn about wines made stronger with grape spirit. You will see why makers add it, how sea trade made these wines famous, and how people drink them today.

items.prompt: Have you ever tried a sweet wine or port? What was it like?
Do you like a drink before a meal, with a meal or after it?
What happens to food or drink when it travels for a long time without a fridge?

blocks.title: Part 1: What Makes a Wine Fortified
paragraphs: Ordinary wine is made by fermentation. Yeast, a tiny living thing, eats the sugar in grape juice and turns it into alcohol. If nothing stops it, the yeast eats almost all the sugar. Then the wine is dry, or not sweet.

A fortified wine is a wine made stronger with spirit. A spirit is a very strong alcoholic drink. It can be made from grain, sugar cane or fruit. The spirit in these wines is made from grapes. Finished port, for example, has about 19 to 22 percent alcohol, much more than ordinary wine.

The first reason for adding spirit was safety. Ordinary wine often went bad on long sea journeys and arrived sour. Strong alcohol protects wine, so fortified wine could spend months in a hot ship and still arrive safely.

The second thing the spirit does depends on when it goes in. Yeast cannot live in such strong alcohol. Picture two barrels of the same grape juice. In the first, makers pour in spirit while fermentation is still going on. The yeast stops, a lot of sugar is left, and the wine stays sweet. This is how port is made. In the second barrel, makers wait until fermentation is over and the sugar is gone. The wine is dry. This is how dry sherry, such as fino, is made. For them, the spirit has a different job: it decides how the wine ages, as you will see later.

images.alt: A winemaker pouring clear grape spirit from a jug into a large wooden vat of dark purple fermenting grape juice

blocks.title: Check: Part 1: What Makes a Wine Fortified

items.prompt: Why is port sweet but fino sherry dry?
items.answer: Port gets its spirit during fermentation, so sugar is left. Fino gets it after fermentation, when the sugar is gone.

blocks.title: Part 2: Fortified Wine and the Sea Trade
paragraphs: These wines became famous thanks to ships and merchants from Britain. Each wine has its own story.

Sherry was the first star. It comes from the area around Jerez, a city in southern Spain. The word sherry is simply the English way of saying Jerez. In 1587 the English sailor Francis Drake attacked Cádiz, a city by the sea not far from Jerez. He carried home about 2,900 barrels of sherry. People in England loved it and called it sack, and it soon became a favourite drink there.

Port came out of a war. In the late 1600s, England and France were enemies, so England stopped buying wine from France. Merchants from England turned to Portugal instead. In 1703 the two countries signed the Methuen Treaty, an agreement about trade. Because of it, wine from Portugal paid much less tax than wine from France. Red wine from the Douro valley in northern Portugal had a long way to go by sea. So the merchants added spirit to keep it safe on the trip. British merchants built this trade. That is why many port houses, the companies that make port, still have British names, such as Taylor's and Graham's.

Madeira is an island of Portugal in the Atlantic Ocean. Ships going to America and Asia often stopped there. Merchants from England lived on the island and ran most of its wine trade. They put barrels of wine on the ships, with spirit added so it would survive. Then something surprising happened. The heat in the hold, the space at the bottom of the ship, made the wine taste better. Wine that travelled the full round trip was called vinho da roda, or wine of the round trip. It became very popular.

images.alt: An old wooden sailing ship in a harbour, with workers rolling wine barrels up a plank onto the deck

items.prompt: Why did English merchants start buying wine in Portugal?
items.answer: England stopped buying wine from France, and because of the Methuen Treaty, wine from Portugal paid less tax.

blocks.title: Part 3: Port, Sherry and Madeira Today
paragraphs: Today each of these wines has one thing that makes it special.

For port, it is the place where it ages. Port grows old in big buildings called lodges. Many of them are in Vila Nova de Gaia, the town across the Douro river from Porto. These lodges stand on the south bank of the river, so they face north, away from the sun. The air inside stays cool and damp, and the wine ages slowly. Some port houses, such as Taylor's, now also have modern lodges in the Douro valley. They keep the same cool, damp air. Visitors who tour a lodge usually try two styles. Ruby port ages only a short time, so it stays bright red and tastes of fresh fruit. Tawny port ages for years in wooden barrels. A little air comes in through the wood, so the wine slowly turns golden brown and tastes of nuts.

For sherry, it is flor, a layer of yeast on top of the wine. It covers the wine in the barrel like a thin white blanket. The flor keeps the air away, so fino and manzanilla stay pale, dry and fresh. But flor can only live if the alcohol is not too strong. So for these wines, makers add only a little spirit, to about 15 percent alcohol. For oloroso, they add more, to about 17 percent. No flor can grow, and air slowly turns the wine dark and rich. A small difference in spirit makes two very different wines.

For Madeira, it is heat. Makers on the island now copy the old ship journey on land. Younger wines are warmed in tanks, and the best wines rest for years in warm rooms. Because the wine has already met heat and air, little can hurt it later. An opened bottle stays good for months.

items.prompt: Why do fino and manzanilla stay pale?
items.answer: Makers add only a little spirit, so flor can live on top and keep the air away.

blocks.title: Part 4: Pineau des Charentes from the Cognac Region
paragraphs: Pineau des Charentes comes from the cognac region in the west of France. It is made in two areas called Charente and Charente-Maritime, and in a small part of the Dordogne. Cognac is the famous strong drink of the region, made from wine. Pineau contains only two things: fresh grape juice and young cognac. Makers use about 3 parts juice for every 1 part cognac. The juice and the cognac must come from the same estate. An estate is the land of one farmer, or of one group of farmers, where the grapes grow.

The cognac goes into the juice before fermentation really starts. This step is called mutage. The strong alcohol stops the yeast, so almost all the grape sugar stays in the drink. That is why Pineau tastes so much of sweet, fresh grapes. A drink made this way, by adding spirit to grape juice, is called a vin de liqueur. Port is different: its juice ferments for a while first, so part of the sugar has already become alcohol. In Japan, umeshu is closer to Pineau, because fruit and sugar sit in strong alcohol and nothing ferments.

Next, Pineau rests in oak barrels. White Pineau ages for at least 18 months, and at least 12 of them must be in oak. Pink and red Pineau, made from red grapes, are sold younger. They taste more of fresh fruit. A Pineau with more than 7 years in oak can be called vieux, or old. With more than 12 years, it is très vieux, or very old.

People in the region tell an old story about how Pineau began. During the harvest of 1589, a farmer poured fresh grape juice into a barrel. He thought it was empty, but some cognac was still inside. Years later he opened the barrel and found a clear, sweet, delicious drink. Pineau was born by accident.

images.alt: Rows of green vines in the Charente countryside in autumn, with a stone farmhouse and oak barrels stacked by its door

blocks.title: Check: Part 4: Pineau des Charentes from the Cognac Region

items.prompt: How is Pineau different from port?
items.answer: In Pineau, the cognac goes in before fermentation really starts. Port ferments for a while before the spirit goes in.

blocks.title: Part 5: How People Drink Fortified Wine Today
paragraphs: People drink each of these wines at the time and the temperature that are best for its taste. Each place has one custom that shows this well.

In the Charente, Pineau is an aperitif, a drink before the meal. Its fresh grape taste is best when it is cold, so people serve it at about 8 to 10 degrees. They do not add ice, because the ice would melt and make the drink weaker. A summer favourite is melon au Pineau. You cut a small Charentais melon in half, take out the seeds and pour Pineau into the middle. The two belong together. The melon is named after the same region, and its sweet fruit matches the sweet grape taste of the drink.

In southern Spain, fino and manzanilla are dry and fresh, and they taste best very cold. People keep the bottle in a bucket of ice and water. These wines are the stars of the spring fairs, such as the famous one in Seville. The wine must stay cold, so people usually order half bottles, not full ones. A half bottle gives about six glasses, so it is empty before it gets warm. So even the last glass is still cold.

In Britain, port is often served at the end of a formal dinner. Its sweet, strong taste is a good way to end the meal. The bottle is passed to the left, so it goes around the table in one direction and reaches everyone. If someone keeps it too long, a guest may ask: Do you know the Bishop of Norwich? A bishop is a church leader, and Norwich is a city in England. One Bishop of Norwich often fell asleep at dinner, so the port stopped next to him. The question is a polite way to say: please pass the bottle.
With Madeira, dry styles are drunk before a meal. Sweet ones come with dessert.
